To install the plugin, click Customize on the left-hand side of the screen, type “equity-research” in the search bar, and click “Add”.
Claude will now show “equity-research” as one of your installed plugins:
To use the commands included in the plugin, start a new chat by clicking “New” at the top-left corner of the screen.
You’ll find the commands when you click “+” at the bottom-left corner of the screen, then “Plugins”, “equity-research” and finally click on the report or model that you want Claude to generate:

Initiate

Model-update

Catalysts

Once you’ve clicked on a command that you want, you’ll be presented with the following screen (just as an example):
You can also just type “/catalysts” followed by the space bar to make the text go blue. After the command, type in the stock ticker and press Enter. Claude will now prepare your report.
Let me now go through exactly what you get in each of the nine commands.
To make the instructions more lively, I’ll use a real-world example of a stock that I’m currently researching: Korean body composition analyzer maker InBody (041830 KS — US$388 million).
The company seems to be benefiting from increased GLP-1 drug usage worldwide, but I have questions about its corporate governance. Let’s see what we can learn.

1. Screener
2. Initiation Report
3. Sector Report
4. Model Update
5. Earnings
6. Earnings Preview
7. Catalyst Calendar
8. Thesis
9. Morning Note
10. Conclusion
Disclosures: As of 18 November 2026, I own shares in Air Water (4088 JP), which appears in the morning-note example. I do not own shares in InBody (041830 KS) or any other company named in this post or its attachments, and do not intend to subscribe to Anthropic’s IPO. I have received no payment, free access or other benefit from Anthropic or any company named here. Asian Century Stocks is published by Delante Media Pte Ltd, Singapore, which is not licensed by MAS to provide financial advice. This post reviews a software tool. The downloadable files are AI output from Claude, with valuation figures removed. They do not represent my views or those of Asian Century Stocks, have not been verified, and are not a recommendation to buy, sell or hold any security.
First, let’s talk about Claude’s screener tool. It lets you search for ideas across any sector, region, or market cap range.
In Claude’s main prompt window, simply type in:
/screen
Claude will ask you a few questions about what kind of screen you want to build.
Alternatively, you can ask for a more specific screen. Since I’m interested in the GLP-1 industry, I might type something along the following lines:
/screen Asian GLP-1 beneficiaries
I then get a 10-page report, with seven stocks listed up front:
The names include InBody at spot number two, and Chinese pharma company United Labs, which coincidentally had a large insider buy in July.
In the report, Claude argues that GLP-1 volumes are likely to rise, so it suggests a picks-and-shovels approach. But it also warns of potential pricing pressure, as we’ve seen in India.
You can download the full GLP-1 screen here:
I think this is an excellent way to unearth new ideas. Of the seven names, five are completely new to me. So I much prefer this type of screen to a quantitative one.
Be aware that the data comes from regular web searches. So if you want higher-quality output, connect Claude to existing paid data sources such as FactSet, LSEG, Capital IQ, etc. To connect these, you may need to install Claude’s financial analysis plugin as well.
Next, we’ll try Claude’s initiate command for initiation reports.
Its initiation reports are typically 6,000 to 8,000 words and cover the company’s history, management team, products, industry, competitive landscape, and risks. It can also give you a financial model with a 5-year projection.
To create an initiation report, simply type in:
/initiate InBody (041830 KS)
I then click “Task 1” to tell Claude to create a report rather than a financial model.
This is the output I then get: a 28-page report with a company overview, company history, and information on the management team, the company’s products, customers, the industry, competitors, and risks.
Beyond the basic report, you can also ask Claude to continue with:
Task 2 (financial model)
Task 3 (valuation)
Task 4 (charts); and
Task 5 (final report)
From the document, I learned that InBody dominates the market for body composition analyzers, which assess weight, muscle, visceral fat, and water levels. I also learned that the company is still run by its founder and chairman, Cha Ki-chul. As it expands in the US, revenue growth has accelerated to a double-digit level. At the same time, Claude points out that there’s new competition from Chinese companies undercutting it on price. But at the higher end of the market for body composition analyzers, InBody seems to be taking market share. The entire industry is also seeing a wave of new demand from GLP-1 patients trying to manage muscle loss.
The report is decent. What’s missing is an analysis of past stock price movements, ownership changes, and what the market might be getting wrong. It failed to mention Naver’s new 8.5% ownership. But it’s a good start.
You can also get Claude to generate a Sector Report. Just type
/sector
followed by the sector you’re interested in.
For example, I’m interested in the body composition analyzer industry. So to understand it better, I simply type:
/sector body composition analyzers
Here’s the report I’m then presented with:
If you’re interested, you can download the full report here:
The report estimates how fast the industry is growing (about 6-10% per year), the different solutions competing for consumers’ attention, and the companies operating in the sector.
I find the report super useful, as it helps me understand each competitor’s strengths and whether InBody is at risk of commoditization. Claude’s answer: potentially, yes.
Next, we’ll generate a financial Model for the stock.
Just type in:
/model-update InBody (041830 KS)
Since I haven’t created a model for InBody yet, I click “Build model now” when prompted, and then ask for an “Excel file” to be generated:
Here’s a screenshot from Claude’s financial model on InBody:
You can download the full model here:
Claude’s model assumes gross margin stays at 76%, which I find a bit aggressive given the risks of competition from Chinese brands. But if Claude’s 2029 earnings-per-share estimate is correct, InBody trades at a 7.5x P/E 2029e earnings.
So can Claude replace a financial analyst for modeling? To some extent, yes. It’s not a full 3-statement model, but it does project future earnings and future cash on the balance sheet.
The problem with Claude’s output is that its estimates are almost identical to those generated by the sell-side analysts that cover the stock. So if you want a variant view on a stock, Claude is unlikely to deliver.
Claude’s Earnings command is a quick way to analyze a company’s latest earnings report. It collects data from public filings, earnings call transcripts, and consensus estimates.
To generate an earnings report, simply type:
/earnings InBody (041830 KS)
I then get the following output:
This report is about 3,000 to 5,000 words and includes a summary, an analysis of the results, a discussion of margins and guidance, what’s changed in the thesis, and, finally, a valuation with internal rate of return estimates.
You can download the report here:
I learned that the USD/KRW exchange rate is a key driver of InBody’s quarterly earnings. Furthermore, Claude projects 13% annual revenue growth for the next four years. It also expects a slight rebound in InBody’s margins. The P/E ratio is low, but the dividend payout ratio is minuscule, and its gift tax issues remain unresolved.
I find the reports a bit lengthy, but exhaustive. I’m sure many of you will find them useful.
The next command, Earnings Preview, helps you prepare for future earnings results. It gives you the reporting date, the consensus estimates, and what management said on the previous call.
To generate an earnings preview, simply type:
/earnings-preview InBody (041830 KS)
And then press Enter. You’re then presented with the following output:
You can download the full report here:
In InBody’s case, it covers factors that will affect the next quarterly result, including the USD/KRW exchange rate. It covers what brokers are forecasting and what might happen to their earnings estimates. For example, many see future GLP-1 partnerships in China and the US hospital segment driving growth.
I personally don’t find these reports particularly helpful, because I don’t trade quarter-to-quarter. But pod shops or traders might find value in them.
Claude’s Catalyst Calendar generates a calendar of future events that are worth tracking.
You can give Claude a single ticker, or an entire portfolio. And specify whether you want it to include macro events or not.
In my case, I type:
/catalysts InBody (041830 KS)
I then get the following catalyst calendar:
These events include the full 3Q2026 earnings (now out), future trade fairs, index rebalancing dates, Bank of Korea/Fed interest rate decisions, and a potential FDA approval of a new Novo Nordisk GLP-1 product.
You can download the full spreadsheet here:
For InBody, I didn’t find this catalyst calendar particularly helpful. But for other stocks, the catalyst calendar has given me great ideas on what to look out for over the next few quarters.
The Thesis command gives you a tracking tool for a particular investment thesis.
It gives you a recommendation (long/short), a 1-2 sentence thesis, 3-5 supporting points, and 3-5 risks, along with catalysts, a target price, and an exit trigger.
To generate a thesis tracker report, I type in the following:
/thesis InBody (041830 KS)
And then get the following output:
Download the full report here:
If you want to update the thesis at any given time, just write “update thesis for InBody (041830 KS): Q3 EPS KRW 12345”, or whatever the new information might be.
From this report, I learned that InBody’s US hospital channel is growing 25% annually and that its US business should now have operating leverage. Claude also argues that increased GLP-1 usage should lead to greater demand for body composition analyzers. Claude sees the Korean won, the costs of hiring additional expats in the US, corporate governance, and Chinese competition as key risks.
Finally, Claude has a Morning Note command that gives you a one-page daily note for a morning meeting.
To generate a note, I type in:
/morning-note
Claude then pulls together the latest news on all of my portfolio holdings. Here’s what the output looks like for me:
The note reminded me about Air Water’s earnings result. It also reminded me about Mercari’s first-quarter result, which sent the stock tanking.
Absolutely. All the grunt work that used to require an actual human — screening for new ideas, writing initiation reports, building financial models, writing morning notes — can now be replaced by Claude and tools like its new Equity Research plugin.
We’ll see how many analysts lose their jobs. I think it’s more likely that fewer analysts will be hired into the profession.
And the analysts who are employed will spend less time on grunt work and more time scanning for new ideas. They’ll then present these ideas to their portfolio managers, who are trying to manage an overflow of information from all sources.
I also believe Claude and other generative AI tools are empowering retail investors in a way never seen before. There are now hordes of retail investors who are just as informed – if not better-informed – than the fund managers they compete with. So there will now be thousands of analysts covering even the smallest stocks. Competition will certainly heat up.
Of Claude’s Equity Research skills, I was particularly impressed by the sector report, the thesis tracker, the catalyst calendar, and the screener. You’ll still need to question what you read and exercise judgment. But Claude can certainly replace much of what we humans have focused on over all these years.
How do you use Claude for research or investing? Let me know in the comment section below:
This article was originally posted here on November 18th, 2026 with some minor edits and additions. This article goes out to all my free readers at a later date.
Finally, learn more about Asian Century Stocks, the publication of our guest contributor today. Supporting other independent bloggers and analysts since 2022.
This is not banking advice but many to most Banks have blocked personal assistants, and for good reason. Like Meta’s Muse. I do not personally recommend giving any AI agent access to your bank account, e.g. using them for shopping activities yet. I know this is confusing for the shopping season, but the technology isn’t there yet.
Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked. Be aware of the risks. Know the terms of your banks. This requires almost a warning statement.
AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments.
At the current time when cybersecurity is not able to keep up with AI, this is not recommended. If financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants.
Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it launched earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.” Beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat so proceed with extreme caution of how you use AI with anything to do with your money, or investing decisions. These tools are extremely nascent, and you should experiment with them only on an ad-hoc and project basis as one tool in your human judgement and those of the professionals who serve your best interests.
For retail investors, analysts and DIY stock pickers, I still think AI and personal finance tools can be extremely valuable. While agentic AI in investing apps are in Beta, you should not rely upon them. For example, Robinhood launched native Agentic Trading and an official Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in mid-to-late 2026. However, there is a wide gap between an AI mechanically executing trades and an AI reliably generating alpha without blowing up an account. I’m not an expert but never allow AI to shop or invest for you, without human-in-the-loop safeguards to the max. Until this technology is fully fleshed out, which may take a while.
I’ll be diving more into Anthropic in future articles, on the IPO performance and the historic impact of this startup in AI in particular. Luckily the community on Subsack has no shortage of these analyses.

Here’s a screenshot from Claude’s financial model on InBody:

You can download the full model here:

Claude’s model assumes gross margin stays at 76%, which I find a bit aggressive given the risks of competition from Chinese brands. But if Claude’s 2029 earnings-per-share estimate is correct, InBody trades at a 7.5x P/E 2029e earnings.

So can Claude replace a financial analyst for modeling? To some extent, yes. It’s not a full 3-statement model, but it does project future earnings and future cash on the balance sheet.

The problem with Claude’s output is that its estimates are almost identical to those generated by the sell-side analysts that cover the stock. So if you want a variant view on a stock, Claude is unlikely to deliver.

5. Earnings

Claude’s Earnings command is a quick way to analyze a company’s latest earnings report. It collects data from public filings, earnings call transcripts, and consensus estimates.

To generate an earnings report, simply type:

/earnings InBody (041830 KS)

I then get the following output:

This report is about 3,000 to 5,000 words and includes a summary, an analysis of the results, a discussion of margins and guidance, what’s changed in the thesis, and, finally, a valuation with internal rate of return estimates.

You can download the report here:

I learned that the USD/KRW exchange rate is a key driver of InBody’s quarterly earnings. Furthermore, Claude projects 13% annual revenue growth for the next four years. It also expects a slight rebound in InBody’s margins. The P/E ratio is low, but the dividend payout ratio is minuscule, and its gift tax issues remain unresolved.

I find the reports a bit lengthy, but exhaustive. I’m sure many of you will find them useful.

6. Earnings Preview

The next command, Earnings Preview, helps you prepare for future earnings results. It gives you the reporting date, the consensus estimates, and what management said on the previous call.

To generate an earnings preview, simply type:

/earnings-preview InBody (041830 KS)

And then press Enter. You’re then presented with the following output:

You can download the full report here:

In InBody’s case, it covers factors that will affect the next quarterly result, including the USD/KRW exchange rate. It covers what brokers are forecasting and what might happen to their earnings estimates. For example, many see future GLP-1 partnerships in China and the US hospital segment driving growth.

I personally don’t find these reports particularly helpful, because I don’t trade quarter-to-quarter. But pod shops or traders might find value in them.

7. Catalyst Calendar

Claude’s Catalyst Calendar generates a calendar of future events that are worth tracking.

You can give Claude a single ticker, or an entire portfolio. And specify whether you want it to include macro events or not.

In my case, I type:

/catalysts InBody (041830 KS)

I then get the following catalyst calendar:

These events include the full 3Q2026 earnings (now out), future trade fairs, index rebalancing dates, Bank of Korea/Fed interest rate decisions, and a potential FDA approval of a new Novo Nordisk GLP-1 product.

You can download the full spreadsheet here:

For InBody, I didn’t find this catalyst calendar particularly helpful. But for other stocks, the catalyst calendar has given me great ideas on what to look out for over the next few quarters.

8. Thesis

The Thesis command gives you a tracking tool for a particular investment thesis.

It gives you a recommendation (long/short), a 1-2 sentence thesis, 3-5 supporting points, and 3-5 risks, along with catalysts, a target price, and an exit trigger.

To generate a thesis tracker report, I type in the following:

/thesis InBody (041830 KS)

And then get the following output:

Download the full report here:

If you want to update the thesis at any given time, just write “update thesis for InBody (041830 KS): Q3 EPS KRW 12345”, or whatever the new information might be.

From this report, I learned that InBody’s US hospital channel is growing 25% annually and that its US business should now have operating leverage. Claude also argues that increased GLP-1 usage should lead to greater demand for body composition analyzers. Claude sees the Korean won, the costs of hiring additional expats in the US, corporate governance, and Chinese competition as key risks.

9. Morning Note

Finally, Claude has a Morning Note command that gives you a one-page daily note for a morning meeting.

To generate a note, I type in:

/morning-note

Claude then pulls together the latest news on all of my portfolio holdings. Here’s what the output looks like for me:

The note reminded me about Air Water’s earnings result. It also reminded me about Mercari’s first-quarter result, which sent the stock tanking.

10. Conclusion

Absolutely. All the grunt work that used to require an actual human — screening for new ideas, writing initiation reports, building financial models, writing morning notes — can now be replaced by Claude and tools like its new Equity Research plugin.

We’ll see how many analysts lose their jobs. I think it’s more likely that fewer analysts will be hired into the profession.

And the analysts who are employed will spend less time on grunt work and more time scanning for new ideas. They’ll then present these ideas to their portfolio managers, who are trying to manage an overflow of information from all sources.

I also believe Claude and other generative AI tools are empowering retail investors in a way never seen before. There are now hordes of retail investors who are just as informed – if not better-informed – than the fund managers they compete with. So there will now be thousands of analysts covering even the smallest stocks. Competition will certainly heat up.

Of Claude’s Equity Research skills, I was particularly impressed by the sector report, the thesis tracker, the catalyst calendar, and the screener. You’ll still need to question what you read and exercise judgment. But Claude can certainly replace much of what we humans have focused on over all these years.

Addendum note on Agents in Banking

This is not banking advice but many to most Banks have blocked personal assistants, and for good reason. Like Meta’s Muse. I do not personally recommend giving any AI agent access to your bank account, e.g. using them for shopping activities yet. I know this is confusing for the shopping season, but the technology isn’t there yet.

Citibank, the third largest commercial bank in the United States, changed its terms of service this week, telling customers who use third-party AI tools for personal finance that anything that goes wrong is their problem — even if they get hacked. Be aware of the risks. Know the terms of your banks. This requires almost a warning statement.

AI agents, ranging from frontier lab models to purpose-built personal finance tools, can be given the credentials to your bank account and other online financial portals, with the idea that they can analyze spending and investment decisions, offer advice, and even handle transactions and bill payments.

At the current time when cybersecurity is not able to keep up with AI, this is not recommended. If financial institutions aren’t thrilled with the unreliable AI actors in their systems, and are telling customers that they won’t be held responsible for reversing an intentional or unintentional transaction made by automated assistants.

Anthropic’s approach is telling: The personal finance tool it launched earlier this month is explicitly billed as “read-only” and “can’t move, manage, or invest your money.” Beyond cybersecurity concerns, banks also view efforts to enter their franchise as a competitive threat so proceed with extreme caution of how you use AI with anything to do with your money, or investing decisions. These tools are extremely nascent, and you should experiment with them only on an ad-hoc and project basis as one tool in your human judgement and those of the professionals who serve your best interests.

For retail investors, analysts and DIY stock pickers, I still think AI and personal finance tools can be extremely valuable. While agentic AI in investing apps are in Beta, you should not rely upon them. For example, Robinhood launched native Agentic Trading and an official Model Context Protocol (MCP) server in mid-to-late 2026. However, there is a wide gap between an AI mechanically executing trades and an AI reliably generating alpha without blowing up an account. I’m not an expert but never allow AI to shop or invest for you, without human-in-the-loop safeguards to the max. Until this technology is fully fleshed out, which may take a while.

Good Morning,
Anthropic’s stock price is now below its IPO price ($83 vs. $81.90 today and falling after hours). It’s an awkward time in the AI cycle and increasingly Anthropic appears to be at the center of it. This comic by Paul Noth in the New Yorker really captures the irony of the times.
As you know, Anthropic was founded in 2021 by former OpenAI employees specifically to prioritize AI safety, alignment, and interpretability. Now nobody talks about what if they fail on their central mission?
After being determined to be the heirs apparent of the AI moniker, with fully weaponized buzzy marketing acronyms like AGI or RSI, and the absolute frontier of AI labs, Anthropic and OpenAI have to actually prove they are good at making real products that people and organizations actually want to use. In many respects, that remains to be seen. So much of how Anthropic views the future of AI seems starkly at odds with making products people need and Enterprise companies use that delivers ROI.
Fast forward nearly six years from their founding and we have a few problems: firstly, Anthropic and OpenAI are facing an increasingly urgent problem supposedly where internal, unreleased models are becoming so powerful that many of their own employees no longer believe they can be safely released, according to Axios’ sources of more than two dozen people familiar with the internal debates.
Now going IPO, the commercial pressure and the supposed internal AI saftey indoctrination of Anthropic, are about to create a lot of pressure and contradictions. All of this is not going to be popular with ordinary Americans and global citizens. It’s already getting chaotic - and why is all of a sudden seemingly everything breaking down?
The same supposedly useful AI is disrupting saftey creating a real-world structural crisis in cybersecurity where Generative AI is uncovering software vulnerabilities at machine speed. In a world where the ROI of Generative AI is in doubt, it’s also embarrassing. AI is being disruptive, but not in the positive market sense.
Secondly, at the same time, the internet is having a Cybersecurity vulnerability apocalypse (for lack of a better term, I’ve seen Vulnpocalypse or Patchpocalypse) due to these models and their actual lack of proper alignment. Microsoft recently has declared a code red in the middle of a ‘Patchpocalypse’. It’s already getting enough doomsday AI for me. But the drama has just begun.
There’s also this little issue of self-replicating AI. What? It really is the stuff of comics and doomsday Netflix documentaries.
“We’re not under attack. Things are just breaking”
Now I just wish Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and others would just focus in 2027 on making great products and applications. In 2027 in a few months we’ll also find out if so-called AI devices are legitimately worth owning for consumers.
At a time when AI coding startups like Cognition are currently in talks to raise (another) $2 billion or more at a $75 billion valuation Anthropic is moving from having Claude write code to helping developers decide when that code is ready to ship. It’s called Claude Ship.
This isn’t RSI, but it’s certainly a step in the right direction to shipping better AI coded products. Claude Ship basically automates and speeds up the post-coding lifecycle on GitHub—specifically reviewing pull requests (PRs), pushing code fixes, and autonomously approving low-risk changes based on team-defined policies.
I expect in 2027 that the intersection of software engineering, product and AI to make significant headway. If Researchers haven't found technical solutions for controlling the most advanced models and they are now under immense commercial pressure to build disruptive products, how will Anthropic cope? It needs to make great products that continues to make Generative AI a must-have for companies of all sizes with models that are actually safe. Anthropic is taunting and flaunting the frontier and it’s not winning many fans with this approach.
Recently an Anthropic mathematician (Levent Alpöge) used an unreleased "research" version of Claude to present a proof of the Riemann hypothesis, which had eluded the brightest human minds for more than 150 years.
I just wish all of the capital being thrown at these companies was leading to great products without the threats and warnings of existential risk, and in such a scenario, perhaps the stock would do better and gain more confidence of investors. If Anthropic keeps making the best models, Claude is going to keep evolving fast.

articles.content:
Good Morning,
I’m still reeling from the AI Boom showing signs of a potential bubble collapse.
To put it into context global and U.S. stock markets just posted their worst week since March 2020 during the week that ended November 20, 2026, driven by a sharp unwinding in AI, Neo Clouds and semi stocks.
Circular financing
Concentration risk
Lack of ROI of Generative AI
Unscrupulous dark budget & margin debt ($1.5 Trillion in 2026)
AI corruption and political upheaval
Capex and rising compute costs
If Nvidia’s controversy is to blame, circular financing and a lack of ROI are top concerns now facing the Generative AI hype train. It’s painful to behold, but Nvidia is facing multiple Federal, State, and internal investigations following the implosion of Nvidia’s stock rising from the resignation of Jensen Huang and the surrounding shady dealings (including a kind of Corporate Nepotism I might add).
This moment in time is a good opportunity and fitting timing to introduce my readers to whose work I have been tracking with some riveted and secret enthusiasm while the manufactured tech optimism on social media is taking a hit. Andi Roach is a rather unique independent researcher, writer, and creator of The Complex Rebel. Drawing on 13 years in enterprise technology, she examines how power and financial incentives shape behavior, reinforce institutional systems, and redistribute risks and consequences across the broader economy.
Nvidia’s situation is certainly an abysmal indication of how far entrenched circular financing abuses and potentially criminal violations go in the high-powered AI economy. This is a watershed moment. All of this changes how we view Anthropic’s IPO as well I might add with its own brand of Silicon Valley controversy. Something is off in AI and suddenly in recent weeks the AI bear position has become more mainstream and as AI sentiment has degenerated significantly in 2026.
One of the reasons Andi’s work intrigues me is how she is able to combine macro and interdisciplinary studies. A former global business strategist and trauma/Complex PTSD (C-PTSD) specialist, she combines systems thinking, psychology, and corporate/financial analysis to examine how power, hierarchy, and trauma operate across institutions and society.
Unfortunately the AI trade and Nvidia in particular, has some similar trauma.
LinkedIn - TikTok - About (click on the links)
Andi based out of Chicago has a fairly appealing working systems framework HTS. She developed Hierarchical Trauma Systems to examine a recurring pattern: the separation of power from the cost of its decisions. Through essays and cultural critique, she translates those dynamics into language people can use.
I personally find this psycho-macro framework rather appealing.
For realism and accountability in AI and systems I really like reads like , and . In fact, many of the women writing about AI on Substack are some of the more interesting critical analysis and critical voices on the topic. I don’t think reading Marcus, Zitron or Burry necessarily gives you the entire picture, with all due respect.
For me it’s difficult to see Nvidia and Anthropic rebounding (at least in the immediate future) from what we just witnessed on the stock market on Friday. This is no ordinary correction.
This could very well be the AI bull market bubble popping. I say this after the extreme downturn of the Friday AI trade. Like historically - on Friday, November 20, 2026, the NASDAQ Composite fell 5.28%, the NASDAQ 100 was down 5.61% and the VIX (fear index) peaked at 39.63. Anything about 30 is rather unusual. This could easily go from something that happens about once a year, to something that happens about once a decade. We’ll know soon enough. Follow the stocks of and and you will know the score.
Andi’s work is more than simply thinking out loud, she trailblazes writing about power, hierarchy, and the systems shaping your life in the AI era. Something American voters have said loud at the ballots and clear matters to them. It matters to us Non-American watching all of this as well. AI power should not be abused.
The Complex Rebel, to the best of my knowledge, examinse corporate consolidation, political dark money, and the financial mechanics of the AI economy. Which is an awesome thing to write about. I wish more people wrote about these topics and like this. It’s highly relatable.
We need investigative journalism, analysts and system thinkers who talk about these elitist agendas because they are spilling over into every aspect of our lives. To some degree without our consent. How Substack Politics and Substack Tech intersects isn’t always optimal. The conversation and news cycle around AI remains full of intrigue.
I pride myself in trying to find a variety of different guest contributors all with their unique voices and angles to give you the very best coverage of AI News and current events in the space. If these sorts of topics and holistic coverage matters to you please enjoy and share.
We need to support independent bloggers, analysts and thinkers.
Please take a look at the following articles:
Meet Your Overlords: The Next Phase Of The AI Economy Is In Your Electricity Bill
Meet Your Overlords: The Influence Economy
Supporting the Complex Rebel and Andi’s work is just $60 a year.
As Venture Capital, PR interests and BigTech lobbying begins to dominate journalism and social media online, I’m seeing all of this in my day job with freaking regularity pushing the internet into a dumpster fire of lower quality and less signal/more noise. This is not the best lens to understand what’s going on, so thank god for Substack. There are still some traces here of genuine introspection.
Now with a breakdown of cybersecurity and the internet’s infrastructure with all of these tech outages recently, it’s a good time to keep score of all the ways and what might end up being the costs of Generative AI to society? They keep adding up. For investors and shareholders this could get wild.
Some context of the financial costs of the last week.
For the trading week ended Friday, November 20, 2026, U.S. equities lost nearly $6 trillion in market value—with roughly $2.4 trillion wiped out on Friday alone as the S&P 500 fell 8.61%
Things are so bad in Asia, Taiwan has moved to significantly tighten short-selling.
Anyways enough of my ranting, let’s get to Andi’s post. It’s 5,000 words or 35k characters. She asked me if I thought it should be edited or trimmed down much, but in this case I want this voice to be heard in its natural state.
I believe we need to question everything about Generative AI and the new fads American Venture Capitalism pushes upon the world.
Profit is real, demand is complicated, and the risks travel a lot further than you think.
As of November 20, 2026. Company figures come from each company’s latest quarterly filing unless noted; market values are as of the dates shown. That day, Reuters, citing two people briefed on the matter, reported an SEC inquiry into Nvidia’s accounting practices, and Nvidia’s stock finished the week down 23%. Nvidia’s figures below are as the company reported them.
Staying up to date on the latest headlines is a feat in itself these days. And when it comes to a topic as complex as the AI economy, it’s hard enough to make sense of what’s happening, let alone figure out how you’re supposed to feel about it. Just look at last week:
“Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.4 trillion in stock market flotation” — The Guardian, November 10.
$1.4 trillion is good, right?
“Sam Altman warns Samsung executives of volatility: ‘AI demand has been double-counted’” — Financial News (South Korea), November 11.
What does that even mean?
“Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns in blow to AI boom he helped foster” — Reuters, November 12.
Uh oh…
And then, of course, we discovered that one man’s affair (make that affairs, one reportedly with a suspected Chinese “spy”) could send one of the world’s most valuable companies into a tailspin. Nvidia lost approximately $573 billion in market value in the week Jensen Huang resigned, proving that when a company is large enough, its CEO’s, uh, “personal crisis” can quickly become a problem sitting in your retirement account.
If you’re already bought into AI, you’ve probably been following these headlines religiously. But if you aren’t, you may be quickly finding out that whether you want to be or not, you’re already a participant in the AI economy.
So… congrats?
You participate through your retirement account, your rising electricity bill, and living through your third “AI transformation” at work this year (also known as “layoffs”). These are decisions made in boardrooms you’ll never see, made by executives you’ll never meet, and they’re actively shaping the conditions of your everyday life.
Yet, we’re still spending more time talking about what AI can do than the economy being built around it.
You may have heard the term circular financing to describe how the companies selling AI are also investing in, financing, or promising to purchase from the very same companies buying from them. And it’s a helpful way to understand how the money moves. But, drawing these relationships as a circle doesn’t fully represent the shape of the AI economy.
Yes, the money loops back around, but those transactions also finance data centers and create debt. Then that financing enables even more expansion; it supports growing valuations, which attracts new investors, and that allows companies to borrow more money and make commitments for years into the future.
The consequences don’t stay inside the circle. Financial gains, ownership, debt, dependencies, and consequences accumulate and change across the system. The next round of decisions begins from the conditions left behind by the last. Circular financing explains how the money moves. The spiral explains what the money changes.
Each revolution can push financial exposure further outward, reaching institutions, investors, utilities, workers, and communities that weren’t part of the original decision-making process.
Who makes the decisions, who realizes the profits, and who carries the risk can look very different depending on where you stand. The closer you are to the center, the more influence you may have over the decisions; at the edges, you may just be trying to survive the fallout.
And unlike a circle, a spiral doesn’t return to the same starting point. Every decision changes the conditions for the next loop. Money gets invested, companies grow, infrastructure gets built, and new financial obligations are created. The companies benefiting from that expansion can gain more resources and influence over what happens next, while the businesses and people carrying the costs have to adapt to decisions already made. And because the benefits and burdens aren’t distributed equally, neither is the power to shape what happens next.
To understand how this works, we have to start where some of the largest profits are realized and follow the money out.
Nvidia designs the chips powering the AI economy. On November 17, it reported $115.8 billion in quarterly revenue, $77.5 billion in operating income, and a ~67% operating margin. That’s 67 cents in profit for every dollar of sales, before taxes and other non-operating items.
Do the rest of the companies in the AI economy make this kind of profit?
Absolutely not.
Yes, Nvidia has competitors like AMD, Broadcom, and Micron, which supply different types of processors and other technology. But Nvidia’s early market lead and years of investment left it uniquely positioned for the AI boom. An enormous part of the industry depends on its hardware and software, giving Nvidia tremendous pricing power and influence over the market. Their revenue is another company’s expense, and profitability starts looking very different depending on which side of the transaction you’re standing on.
When Nvidia delivers its product, satisfying the accounting requirements for a sale, the revenue is recorded immediately. Even if they collect payment later, Nvidia doesn’t have to wait six years to recognize the sale from equipment that the buyer on the other side of that transaction might depreciate over that time. And for a company like CoreWeave, buying Nvidia equipment is only the beginning.
It has to finance the purchase, install the hardware, get the systems operational, and find the customers to generate enough revenue over time to recover its investment.
CoreWeave currently depreciates the GPUs it buys over an estimated six-year useful life.
That means the accounting expense is spread across the years the equipment is expected to be used. The actual money needed to buy it, whether supplied by investors, lenders, customers, or the company itself, has to be available much, much sooner. And the costs to finance that money arrive with it.
So, Nvidia makes its sale and then uses the resulting earnings to invest in the next opportunity. The company buying the equipment, like CoreWeave, has to keep generating revenue just to justify the purchase, while also managing the possibility that newer technology, changing prices, or slowing demand could make that investment less valuable than expected.
One company’s profit becomes another company’s long-term bet.
Frontier AI developers like OpenAI and Anthropic build the models that people and businesses use. Running these models requires a huge amount of computing capacity, which they purchase from cloud and infrastructure providers. And demand for those services is real. Consumers pay for subscriptions. Just like businesses pay for enterprise services, and developers pay to integrate the models into their products. But companies are building infrastructure to support current demand plus how much demand they expect to have in the future.
And there’s a big difference between demand and anticipated demand.
Take OpenAI. In October 2025, it committed to purchase an additional $250 billion in Microsoft Azure services. That’s a massive commitment based on—what, exactly? Certainly not $250 billion in cash OpenAI already collected from customers who will eventually use that computing capacity.
The agreement reflects expectations about future demand, future revenue, and OpenAI’s ability to finance those purchases along the way. Microsoft, in turn, can use that commitment to inform its own infrastructure and investment decisions. And Microsoft isn’t OpenAI’s only infrastructure provider. OpenAI also contracts with Oracle, CoreWeave, and other companies to secure the computing capacity it expects to need.
Then what happens?
One AI developer commits to buying infrastructure services. Then multiple suppliers get expectations of future revenue. Those suppliers then buy the equipment, build the infrastructure, get financing, and make their own commitments to deliver the services. One AI developer’s forecast becomes another company’s business opportunity—and potentially another company’s financial obligation. And with every new commitment, companies put more money and infrastructure behind the expectation that this future demand will actually materialize.
Which brings us to a rather concerning headline from South Korea’s Financial News. According to materials obtained from an October 31 meeting with Samsung executives, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman acknowledged that parts of the AI market had “double-counted” demand, particularly around memory chips and data centers. By his count, the big increase in demand comes from just two companies: OpenAI and Anthropic.
So, what does that actually mean?
On November 16, on stage at a Semafor conference, the explanation came from Altman himself: every chip supplier is planning to sell to the same few buyers, and those buyers won’t be buying from all of them.
Several suppliers can build for the same customer. Not all of them get the business. And we’ve already watched it happen.
By early 2025, about 2 gigawatts of planned Microsoft data-center projects had disappeared from the pipeline, according to analysts at TD Cowen, who traced most of it to Microsoft’s decision not to take on more of OpenAI’s training work. OpenAI took that business to other providers, including Oracle. Then in March 2026, the planned expansion of Oracle and OpenAI’s flagship Texas data center fell apart, with financing talks stalled and OpenAI’s own capacity plans shifting. A $150 million deposit from Nvidia reportedly held the space while Meta weighed taking it instead. (By Oracle’s account, the rest of its OpenAI build is proceeding as planned.)
Other buyers showed up for some of that space, so none of this proves the demand is fake. It shows that demand can move while the buildings can’t.
And then account for what companies report to investors. At the end of September 2026, Microsoft reported $677 billion in commercial remaining performance obligations. Oracle reported approximately $664 billion at the end of August. CoreWeave reported $132.5 billion in revenue backlog at September 30. These companies use different accounting measures, but the numbers generally describe revenue they expect to recognize from customer commitments over time (they are not guaranteed profits, and they do not tell us how much additional demand will come from the people and businesses ultimately buying).
These totals include different customers, products, time periods, and contractual terms. And we can’t just add them all up and say they’re all OpenAI or assume they prove double counting. But they definitely should raise a few eyebrows. Because how much of the demand traces back to the same customer expectations of future growth and how would we ever be able to tell?
A commitment to purchase computing capacity isn’t the same as a customer actually using and paying for that capacity. And the suppliers building infrastructure around those commitments still need to deliver their services, cover their costs, and collect the revenue in the process. And that financial exposure can be a massive risk. A large customer contract can help an infrastructure provider get that financing for expansion. But the provider still needs to buy equipment, build or lease facilities, and take on financial obligations before it earns that expected revenue.
And that risk becomes especially important for companies borrowing heavily to support a handful of huge customers. Because if demand is slower than expected, or one customer changes their mind, those companies still have to pay the financing and operating costs of the infrastructure they committed to build.
The commitment creates business for the next company—and—it influences what that company finances, purchases, and builds. The system loops back around, but the starting point has changed. Each agreement shapes the conditions for the next.
Nvidia’s customers need money to buy its chips. And Nvidia is all about supporting them to make that happen. Hence the nickname, The Bank of Nvidia.
In its November 17 financial disclosures, Nvidia reported approximately $61.7 billion in privately held equity investments and $44.2 billion in marketable equity securities. Those figures represent the carrying values of investments (not cash profits Nvidia collected from selling them, and not every investment directly finances a chip customer), but the scale shows just how far Nvidia’s financial interests extend beyond selling hardware. And its involvement doesn’t stop there.
Nvidia also agreed to provide guarantees capped at $105 billion to support the development of SB Energy’s PORTS-Pike data-center campus in Ohio, which plans to lease computing infrastructure to OpenAI. The guarantees take effect in phases as the buildings become ready for service, and Nvidia would face payment obligations if certain conditions trigger them. But that’s also what makes the arrangement notable. Nvidia can use its financial strength to support an enormous infrastructure project before the expected revenue from that project materializes.
And in August, Nvidia announced partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to develop financing platforms aimed at mobilizing more than $500 billion in third-party capital for AI infrastructure over time. The company selling the technology is helping organize the capital that will finance the infrastructure needed to purchase and use more of it.
The supplier helps create the financial conditions that make the next round of growth possible.
And other companies are following suit. Amazon invested $8 billion in Anthropic convertible notes between 2023 and 2025. In its September 2026 financial statements, Amazon valued its remaining convertible notes at approximately $146.2 billion. A pretty incredible paper gain, which they don’t need to realize to benefit from that holding. They also invested another $10 billion in Anthropic preferred stock during 2026.
Amazon also happens to provide cloud computing services Anthropic needs to develop and operate its models. So, Anthropic receives capital to fund its growth. Amazon earns revenue from cloud services and stands to benefit if its Anthropic investments increase in value. And Anthropic’s demand for computing capacity helps justify additional infrastructure spend. These arrangements depend on interconnected expectations about future growth of the same market.
One company’s growth creates revenue opportunities for another, while the financing behind that growth can give the supplier a direct stake in its customer’s success.
And we’re talking about huge amounts of capital flowing through these relationships. On November 16, Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr described more than $100 billion in cumulative equity investments by major chipmakers and hyperscalers into AI developers and cloud startups. He also noted those investments represent a relatively small share of the largest companies’ balance sheets, but they can be critical to the smaller companies receiving the money. Because the same financial relationship can mean very different things depending on which side of it you’re standing on.
Accounting rules require a company to disclose when a single customer makes up 10% or more of its revenue, which is why we know CoreWeave accounts for 93% of Core Scientific’s. But the test is measured against a company’s size. The same contract that is nearly everything to the smaller company can be a rounding error to the larger one. Microsoft doesn’t break out what it spends with CoreWeave. Nvidia doesn’t name its customers at all. So the public can see the dependence, but only from the side that’s carrying it.
A large supplier can invest in a customer, earn revenue from selling it equipment or services, and potentially benefit from the value of its ownership stake increasing. The customer gains access to capital—and—it also takes on the risk of generating enough future revenue to sustain its growth.
The infrastructure providers supporting those customers face their own financial obligations as well. Nvidia’s guarantees create contingent exposure, and of course, equity investments can lose value. But they also have different resources, access to capital, and the ability to absorb a setback.
A successful investment increases a company’s financial resources. A large computing contract can help another company get financing. That financing supports additional construction, creating more orders for equipment and more business for the companies supplying it. Suppliers become investors. Customers become financial partners. Financial institutions develop new ways to fund the expansion.
That’s how the spiral starts reinforcing itself.
The companies accumulating profits, ownership, and financial influence gain more opportunities to shape where capital flows next. Meanwhile, other participants accumulate the obligations required to deliver on those expectations. The broader system becomes more and more dependent on continued growth.
Meanwhile, someone still has to take on the obligations required to turn those financial commitments into actual computing capacity. And at some point, all that money has to become something physical.
While “the cloud” sounds like some wonderfully weightless place floating around in space, it’s actually super physical. We’re talking massive buildings filled with processors, cooling systems, and thousands of servers using extraordinary amounts of power. And someone has to finance the construction long before those assets generate all the revenue companies expect them to produce.
JLL estimates that data-center construction will average $11.3 million per megawatt globally in 2026, before companies even install the computing equipment. For AI infrastructure, the technology fit-out can add as much as another $25 million per megawatt. Securing enough power can take years, on timelines set by utilities and regulators rather than the developers themselves. Which helps explain why even companies like Meta, with billions in profits and years of experience building data centers, increasingly turn to outside developers and financiers–a strategy that spreads the risks and costs of construction across the companies supplying capital, equipment, real estate, and electricity, often through contracts that extend years into the future.
Enter CoreWeave, a specialized cloud provider, or neocloud, which rents computing capacity to AI developers and other customers that don’t want to own the infrastructure themselves.
In its third quarter, CoreWeave generated $3.66 billion in revenue, up 168% year over year, with $207 million in operating income, $846 million in net interest expense, and a $709 million net loss. The company earned an operating profit, but its net interest expense alone was more than four times that amount. By September 30, CoreWeave carried approximately $47.5 billion in debt principal against $132.5 billion in revenue backlog.
Backlog is essentially revenue that CoreWeave expects to earn delivering computing services under customer commitments. But CoreWeave still needs to deliver the capacity, cover its operating expenses, and collect payments to do that over time. And with tens of billions in debt, the company has considerably less margin for error when refinancing becomes difficult or the demand supporting its expansion falls short of expectations.
Which brings us right back to Nvidia.
CoreWeave builds its GPU infrastructure around Nvidia hardware, and Nvidia has a financial stake in CoreWeave’s continued expansion. In January 2026, Nvidia invested another $2 billion in CoreWeave stock. The companies also entered a capacity agreement in September 2025, initially valued at $6.3 billion, giving Nvidia access to qualifying computing capacity that CoreWeave doesn’t sell to other customers. So Nvidia sells the hardware, owns a stake in the company buying it, and provides a contractual backstop for some of its unsold capacity. The agreement helps support CoreWeave’s business, and it also creates exposure for Nvidia if CoreWeave can’t sell that capacity elsewhere.
But their financial positions within that arrangement are wildly different. Nvidia generates enormous profits selling the technology that powers the expansion. CoreWeave borrows billions to purchase and operate that technology, depending on a future where it has enough computing revenue to recover its investment and service its debt.
CoreWeave carries financial exposure from its relationship with Nvidia, while making commitments that create dependencies for the companies supplying the physical infrastructure beneath it. Take Core Scientific for example. They’re a former cryptocurrency miner that now develops and operates data centers for AI infrastructure. In its third-quarter disclosures, Core Scientific reported that just one customer accounted for 93% of its total quarterly revenue. And that customer was CoreWeave.
In May, Core Scientific raised $3.3 billion through senior secured notes carrying a 7.75% interest rate, using the proceeds in part to refinance earlier borrowing and establish debt-service reserves. They also contracted approximately 590 megawatts of capacity to CoreWeave, representing only about 13% of CoreWeave’s more than 4.6 gigawatts of contracted power. And while revenue for Core Scientific and contracted power for CoreWeave measure different things, they show an imbalance in the relationship: Core Scientific depends on CoreWeave for nearly all its current revenue, while CoreWeave uses infrastructure from many different providers.
So, what happens if CoreWeave delays a project or runs into financial trouble?
Core Scientific already took out loans and built the infrastructure for their customer making up almost all of their revenue. At September 30, only 485 megawatts of its 590-megawatt commitment to CoreWeave had begun generating billable revenue. The remaining capacity was still moving through construction and commissioning. And its ability to absorb a setback depends heavily on the financial health of the one customer it relies on.
In the meantime, CoreWeave faces its own dependencies on AI developers, hardware suppliers, lenders, and investors. It can hold bargaining power over one provider while being financially exposed to decisions made by its own customers and financiers. The same company can absorb instability from one part of the economy and create financial consequences for another.
Then, we need to talk about time. We mentioned previously that CoreWeave depreciates computing equipment over an estimated six-year useful life. Customer payment terms, their lender’s repayment schedule, and other agreements may be on completely different schedules. They have to manage overlapping timelines regardless of what happens to demand, plus take into consideration the six-year depreciation estimate doesn’t actually guarantee six years of profitable use.
A company can face instability for a variety of reasons—changing demand, cost of capital, new regulations, whatever—and not every company has the same ability to respond. The financial exposure remains even when the expectations that justified it change.
And suddenly, the separation between who makes the decisions and who bears the consequences becomes much easier to see. An AI developer’s forecast influences a cloud provider’s plans to build infrastructure. The cloud provider signs contracts, buys hardware, and gets financing. Infrastructure developers commit capital to facilities that may take years to complete and even longer to pay off. By the time those decisions become physical assets, multiple companies have tied their financial futures to expectations that originated somewhere else in the system. Each relationship creates opportunities for some participants and obligations for others, changing the financial conditions under which they make their next decisions.
The farther we move from the original chip sale, the more companies, creditors, physical assets, and long-term commitments become involved. And the consequences don’t necessarily end at the businesses that signed the contracts.
The financial gains are easy enough to see because they’re sitting on Nvidia’s income statement. Lenders earn interest under their agreements, and investors watch their holdings appreciate, sometimes dramatically. But we’re measuring the economic benefits of AI by how much money the industry makes.
In a November 9 speech, the Reserve Bank of Australia reported that approximately 35% of businesses in its liaison survey saw no productivity gains from AI, while another 30% reported only minor improvements. Others reported moderate or significant gains, so the technology clearly has practical applications. But those benefits remain uneven, and we’re still only learning how benefits will materialize while AI suppliers are bringing in record profits.
And the costs are being realized too. We just have to follow the infrastructure a little farther.
When a company commits to building or leasing a new data center, that facility needs power, and lots of it. Utilities and grid operators factor anticipated demand into forecasts and investment plans, potentially requiring new electrical infrastructure. Who ultimately pays depends on contracts and regulatory decisions made in each market. Infrastructure built around anticipated demand has the potential to leave behind decades of expenses, even if the projects that originally justified those investments never materialize.
In Illinois, consumer advocates reported that ComEd’s October 2026 electricity supply price was 53% higher than two years earlier, with increased data center demand as a major contributing factor. WBEZ reported that ComEd has $3.1 billion in anticipated grid infrastructure costs associated with 30 projects. Meaning consumers could inherit some of those costs if projects fall through. ComEd disputes that characterization, and the eventual allocation will depend on these agreements and regulatory decisions.
Data-center developers negotiate locations, contracts, and construction, while utilities and regulators get to decide how electrical infrastructure is built and how to recover those costs. Us people at home have a lot less say in those decisions, and we end up living with the consequences.
And then there are the costs that don’t arrive as bills.
Researchers working with Pima County and Johns Hopkins identified air quality, water consumption, noise, heat, and health impacts that warrant assessment around data-center development. A company can calculate its electricity and construction costs down to the dollar while the surrounding community faces questions about clean water, air pollution, noise, and long-term health effects that are considerably harder to quantify.
Then there’s employment.
A corporation can announce an AI-driven efficiency initiative, cut payroll expenses, and report cost savings before anyone knows whether the technology actually delivers better outcomes. Challenger, Gray & Christmas counted more than 121,000 U.S. job cuts through October where the employer gave AI as the reason, more than twice last year’s full-year total. Yet the RBA’s own survey of Australian firms found headcount unchanged by AI at roughly three in four of them. The announcement and the technology are not the same thing. The executives making those decisions have much more control over the timing and allocation of resources than the workers who have to live with the loss of stability, loss of income, and increased workloads for the workers left behind. The workers must adapt to conditions they did not make.
Businesses reorganize around AI tools; employees learn new systems, change how they work, or leave altogether. Software providers respond to what companies purchase, investors finance the businesses they expect to grow, and employers make new decisions based on the outcomes of their earlier investments.
And the financial risks extend even further. The Federal Reserve’s November Financial Stability Report identifies rapid growth in AI-related borrowing, circular financing networks, and complex financial obligations as potential sources of instability. The same report locates most of the hyperscalers’ and chipmakers’ debt in mutual funds, pension funds, and insurance companies. That’s how those exposures can reach the retirement accounts of people who never chose to finance the AI buildout.
The gains and the costs aren’t realized by the same people, in the same places, at the same time.
And those differences are important because the system doesn’t reset after each round of investment. Companies adjust their business plans, workers change how they earn a living, households adapt to higher costs, and infrastructure providers continue servicing commitments they made under earlier assumptions. The people and institutions absorbing those consequences enter the next round with different resources, obligations, and choices than they had before. And the system continues investing, borrowing, building, and adapting.

Meet Your Overlords: An Introduction to the AI Economy

Profit is real, demand is complicated, and the risks travel a lot further than you think.
